part: Part A: the floor you cannot skip
title: Powers of Ten, Prefixes, Constants and the Seven Steps
lead: Almost every mark lost on this paper is lost before the physics starts. Five of the fifteen options in a PHY121 question are usually the SAME digits with different powers of ten, so the exponent is the thing being marked. This lesson makes that automatic.

blocks.html:
Start with something you already know. A millimetre is a thousandth of a metre. Nobody finds that hard. Every prefix in this course is that same idea wearing a different coat.

Now look at what the examiner actually does with it.

  1. Test 2 question 8 offers you five answers: 7.58 x 10-4, 7.58 x 10-6, 7.58 x 10-2, 7.58 x 10-8, 7.58 x 10-1.
  2. Read them again. The digits are identical. Only the power of ten changes.
  3. So the physics is already given to you. The examiner has decided to mark exactly one thing.
Key point

When five options share the same digits, the exponent IS the question. The mark is not for knowing the formula. It is for handling the powers of ten.

Your turn, before you read on. If a question gives you 8 mg, what is that in kilograms?

Given
8 mg
Step 1, milli means 10-3
8 mg = 8 x 10-3 g
Step 2, a gram is itself 10-3 kg
= 8 x 10-3 x 10-3 kg
Answer
= 8 x 10-6 kg

It needs BOTH conversions. Most people do one and stop.

So far, so good. That single slip is worth a mark on Test 1 question 3, and this lesson exists to make it impossible.

The three that appear constantly in PHY121: micro for charge and capacitance, nano for small capacitors and charges, pico for the smallest capacitors.

blocks.label: The four constants, and where each one lives
blocks.html:
Four numbers run through the whole course. Learn them with the formula they belong to, never as a bare list, because that is how the exam gives them to you.

ConstantSymbolValueLives in
Coulomb constantk8.99 x 109 N m2 C-2, used as 9 x 109F = kq1q2/r2, E = k|Q|/r2, V = kQ/r
Permittivity of free spaceε08.85 x 10-12 F m-1Gauss, capacitors, the speed of light
Elementary chargee1.602 x 10-19 Cq = ne, and every charge on an electron or proton
Permeability of free spaceµ04π x 10-7 H m-1Every magnetic source formula. Met properly in Part E
The link worth seeing early

k and ε0 are the same constant twice: k = 1/(4πε0). Put 8.85 x 10-12 into that and you get 8.99 x 109 back. So a question that hands you one has handed you both.

Two of them are electric and one is magnetic. ε with an E sound for electric, µ for magnetic. That pairing is all you need to keep them apart, and in the last lesson of this course the two of them multiply together to give the speed of light.

Leave µ0 as 4π x 10-7. Do not convert it to 1.2566 x 10-6. The π almost always cancels against a π in the formula, and cancelling is faster and safer than multiplying.

blocks.label: The centimetre trap
blocks.html:
A distance in centimetres squared is the single most expensive slip in this course. Test 1 question 4 gives r = 5 cm. If you put 5 into kQ/r you get a potential 100 times too small, and 20 cm gives one 400 times too small.

5 cm is 0.05 m, and 0.05 squared is 0.0025. Convert the moment you read the number, before you write anything else down. That is step 3 of the seven steps, and it is the step that saves the most marks.

blocks.label: Powers of ten, one step at a time
blocks.tag: cover the page and slide down
blocks.howto: Read the teaching step, do the small task at the end of it, then move to the next frame, which opens with the answer. Do not read ahead.

frames.teach: To multiply powers of ten, ADD the exponents. 10<sup>3</sup> times 10<sup>4</sup> is 10<sup>7</sup>.
frames.ask: What is 2 x 10<sup>-6</sup> multiplied by 3 x 10<sup>-3</sup>?

frames.check: 6 x 10<sup>-9</sup>. Multiply the front numbers, 2 times 3 = 6, then add the exponents, minus 6 plus minus 3 = minus 9.
frames.teach: To divide, SUBTRACT the bottom exponent from the top one. 10<sup>5</sup> divided by 10<sup>2</sup> is 10<sup>3</sup>.
frames.ask: What is 8 x 10<sup>-4</sup> divided by 4 x 10<sup>-7</sup>?

frames.check: 2 x 10<sup>3</sup>. Divide the front numbers, 8 over 4 = 2, then subtract, minus 4 minus minus 7 = plus 3.
frames.teach: Watch what happens when the front division gives less than 1. 3.64 over 4.8 is 0.758, which is NOT in standard form, so you shift it to 7.58 and drop the exponent by one to compensate.
frames.ask: Work out (9.1 x 10<sup>-31</sup> x 4 x 10<sup>6</sup>) divided by (1.6 x 10<sup>-19</sup> x 0.03), which is Test 2 question 8.

frames.check: 7.58 x 10<sup>-4</sup> m. Top: 9.1 x 4 = 36.4, and minus 31 plus 6 = minus 25, so 36.4 x 10<sup>-25</sup>, that is 3.64 x 10<sup>-24</sup>. Bottom: 1.6 x 0.03 = 0.048, so 4.8 x 10<sup>-21</sup>. Dividing: 3.64 over 4.8 = 0.758 and minus 24 minus minus 21 = minus 3, giving 0.758 x 10<sup>-3</sup> = 7.58 x 10<sup>-4</sup>.
frames.teach: That last shift, from 0.758 x 10<sup>-3</sup> to 7.58 x 10<sup>-4</sup>, is exactly the step the five options were testing.

frames.check: 10<sup>-4</sup>. The less negative the exponent, the bigger the number. 10<sup>-4</sup> is a ten thousandth, 10<sup>-6</sup> a millionth.
frames.teach: Keep the front numbers and the powers of ten in two separate columns while you work. That is step 6 of the seven-step method, and it is what stops the exponent slipping.

blocks.label: The seven steps
blocks.html:
1. Read the question twice and underline what is asked for. Marks are lost every paper answering a question that was not set.
  2. List what you know, with symbols and units, and write the unknown with a question mark next to it.
  3. Convert everything to SI immediately: centimetres to metres, microfarads to farads, milligrams to kilograms.
  4. Choose the formula holding what you know and what you want. If no single formula does, you need an intermediate step.
  5. Rearrange in symbols first, and substitute numbers only at the end.
  6. Compute, keeping the powers of ten separate from the front numbers.
  7. Check: is the size believable, is the unit right, does the sanity check hold?
Learn the seven as one word

Read, list, convert, choose, rearrange, compute, check.
Steps 3 and 7 save the most marks and are the two most often skipped, because they are the two that feel like they are not really doing physics.

blocks.label: Your turn
blocks.question:
Convert each to SI: (1) 8 mg, (2) 50 cm, (3) 4.5 nC, (4) 2.25 mJ, (5) 5 pF.

Then, without looking back: what is k, and what is e?
blocks.answer:
(1) 8 x 10-6 kg, because milli is 10-3 and a gram is 10-3 kg. (2) 0.50 m. (3) 4.5 x 10-9 C. (4) 2.25 x 10-3 J. (5) 5 x 10-12 F.

Number 1 catches people twice, because milligrams need BOTH conversions. It is Test 1 question 3.

k = 8.99 x 109 N m2 C-2, used as 9 x 109. e = 1.602 x 10-19 C. If either was slow to come, say them aloud three times now. They appear in more questions than any other numbers on the paper.

title: Charge, Conductors and Coulomb's Law
lead: Everything electrical starts with two facts: charge comes in whole coins, and two charges push or pull along a line between them. Get those and the inverse square law stops being something to memorise.

blocks.text: What charge is, before any formula

blocks.label: Coins, not liquid
blocks.html:
Start with money. You can hold 3 naira or 4 naira. You cannot hold 3.7 naira in coins, because there is a smallest coin and everything is a whole number of them.

Charge behaves in exactly that way. There is a smallest coin, the charge on one electron, and every charge you will ever meet is a whole number of those.

q = ne (q the total charge in coulombs, n the NUMBER of electrons or protons, always a whole number, e the elementary charge = 1.602 x 10-19 C)

Key point

Charge comes in coins, not in liquid. You never meet half an electron's worth. That is what the word quantised means, and n is a plain count with no unit at all.

The second fact is the one every child discovers with a balloon and their hair.

  • Like repels. Two positives push apart. Two negatives push apart.
  • Unlike attracts. A positive and a negative pull together.

Trivial as it sounds, it decides the sign of every force answer in Part B, and in the field lesson it will decide whether two fields add or cancel.

Your turn. A system carries 6.2 x 1018 electrons. What is its charge?

Given
n = 6.2 x 1018
e = 1.602 x 10-19 C
Formula
q = ne
Substitute
q = 6.2 x 1018 x 1.602 x 10-19
front: 6.2 x 1.602 = 9.93
exponents: 18 plus minus 19 = minus 1
Answer
q = 9.93 x 10-1 = 0.99 C

That is Test 1 question 10.

Notice the answer sits just under 1 coulomb. That is not a coincidence: 1 divided by e is about 6.24 x 1018, so 6.2 x 1018 electrons is very nearly one coulomb exactly. Keep that as a free check.

Say it bluntly

n is a count. It has no unit and it is never a fraction.

blocks.label: Conductors and insulators
blocks.html:
Two words that will come back in Gauss's law, in capacitors and in circuits, so learn them once here.

WordWhat it meansEveryday case
ConductorCharge moves freely through itCopper wire, the metal body of a car
InsulatorCharge is bound and cannot move freelyRubber, glass, dry air, plastic
Key point

The whole difference is whether the charge can walk about. In a conductor it can, so any excess charge runs to the outer surface and spreads out. In an insulator it is stuck where you put it.

That one sentence explains three later results in advance:

  1. Charge on a conductor sits on the outside, which is why the field inside a hollow conductor is zero.
  2. An insulator between capacitor plates cannot carry current, which is what lets a capacitor hold a voltage at all.
  3. A conductor's resistance is low precisely because the charge is free to move.

Your turn. Lightning strikes a car with you inside it. Why are you safe?

Because the car body is a conductor.

Charge runs to the outer surface
so no charge is enclosed inside
so there is no field inside
so nothing pushes current through you

It is not the rubber tyres. The metal shell is doing the work, and you will prove it with Gauss's law in Part B.

blocks.label: Coulomb's law
blocks.html:
F = k q1 q2 / r2

SymbolMeaningUnit
FForce between the two charges, along the line joining themnewton, N
q1, q2The TWO charges. A force needs two objects to act betweencoulomb, C
rDistance between them, in METRES, and it is squaredmetre, m
kCoulomb's constant8.99 x 109 N m2 C-2
The hook for the inverse square

Triple the distance and the force drops to a NINTH.
Not a third. The r is squared, so 3 becomes 9, 4 becomes 16, 10 becomes 100.
Halve the distance and the force goes up FOUR times.

Why squared, in one picture. Whatever the charge sends out spreads over the surface of a sphere, and a sphere's area is 4πr2. Double the radius and the same amount is spread over four times the area, so what arrives at any one spot is a quarter. Gravity thins out in exactly the same way, for exactly the same reason.

Two charges, always. If a question hands you only one charge, Coulomb's law is not the formula it wants. That is the single most useful thing to notice about it, and the next lesson is built on it.

blocks.label: Superposition: one at a time, then add
blocks.tag: the method for every multi-charge question
blocks.html:
Start with a tug of war. Three people pull on you at once. How do you work out where you end up? You do not invent a three-person formula. You take each pull separately, then add the pulls as arrows.

Charges work the same way, and the rule has a name.

Superposition

Compute one contribution at a time, then add. It works for forces, for fields and for potentials alike, and it is the only method you need for every multi-charge question on this paper.

There is one difference between the three, and it matters:

QuantityVector or scalarHow you add
Force FVectorAs arrows, direction matters
Field EVectorAs arrows, direction matters
Potential VScalarPlain arithmetic, signs and all

Your turn. Two charges sit either side of a point. Their fields there are 1.08 x 107 N/C each. What is the net field?

You cannot answer yet.

The sizes are not enough.
If both arrows point the same way: 2.16 x 107 N/C
If they point opposite ways: 0

You have to draw the directions first. The next lesson gives you a picture that makes that automatic.

blocks.label: Your turn
blocks.question:
(1) A charge of 4.8 x 10-19 C. How many elementary charges is that, and is the answer allowed?

(2) Two charges 2 cm apart feel a force of 36 N. What force do they feel at 6 cm?

(3) Why can Coulomb's law never be used with a single charge?
blocks.answer:
(1) n = q/e = 4.8 x 10-19 / 1.602 x 10-19 = 3 electrons. A whole number, so it is allowed. An answer of 3.4 would mean an arithmetic slip, because charge comes in coins.

(2) Three times the distance, so a NINTH of the force. 36/9 = 4 N. Notice you never needed the charges or k: the ratio was the whole question.

(3) Because a force acts BETWEEN two objects. One charge on its own has nothing to push against. What one charge does have is a field, and that is the next lesson.

blocks.sub: And triple the distance means a ninth of the force.

title: The Electric Field: One Charge, Not Two
lead: The single most common error on this paper is putting the wrong charge into the formula. This lesson makes the choice automatic, and gives you a picture that decides direction without any algebra.

blocks.label: What a field actually is
blocks.html:
Start with something you have felt. Hold two magnets near each other and you feel a push before they touch. Nothing crosses the gap that you can see, yet the force is real.

Electric charges do the same thing, and the explanation is worth getting exactly right.

  1. A charge does not reach out and touch another charge.
  2. It changes the space around it.
  3. A second charge, placed in that space, responds to the space it finds itself in.

That change in the space is what we call the electric field.

Key point

Because the field belongs to the space, there are always TWO questions, never one. What field is there? And what force does a charge feel in it?

QuestionDepends onFormula
What field is there?Only the charge producing itE = k|Q|/r2 (E the field, Q the charge producing it, r your distance from it in metres, k = 9 x 109)
What force does a charge feel?The field, and the charge sitting in itF = qE (F the force in newtons, q the charge sitting in the field, in coulombs)

Your turn. Test 1 question 13 gives two charges and asks for the field produced by the NEGATIVE one, at the location of the positive one. Which charge goes into the formula?

Answer: only the negative one.

The positive charge is where you are standing, not what you are measuring.

Given
Q = 2.0 x 10-8 C (the negative charge, magnitude)
r = 0.40 m
k = 9 x 109
Formula
E = k|Q|/r2
Substitute
E = (9 x 109 x 2.0 x 10-8) / (0.40)2
E = 180 / 0.16
Answer
E = 1125 N/C

Use the other charge instead and you get roughly four times this, which is one of the five options offered.

Say it bluntly

Only the charge PRODUCING the field goes in the formula.

blocks.label: The four formulas
blocks.html:
QuantityFormulaNote
Quantisationq = nen a whole number
Coulomb's lawF = kq1q2/r2Between two charges
FieldE = F/q = k|Q|/r2Vector
PotentialV = kQ/rScalar. Note the plain r

What every letter means

SymbolMeaningUnit
QThe charge producing the field. One charge, not twocoulomb, C
qThe charge sitting in a field and feeling a forcecoulomb, C
| |Bars mean magnitude: use the size of the charge and drop the minus signsame as what is inside
nNumber of electrons or protons, always a whole numbernone, it is a count

Read r carefully. It is always a distance in METRES, so 5 cm must become 0.05 before it goes anywhere near the formula, and in E and F it is then squared.

blocks.label: One charge or two, and why the bars are there
blocks.html:
Start with the wind. Ask two different questions about it. How strong is it? That answer is a size: 30 km/h. Which way is it blowing? That answer is a direction: from the east.

You would never answer the first question with "minus 30 km/h". Strength has no sign. The sign belongs to the direction, and you state it separately.

Electric formulas work the same way, and that is what the bars in E = k|Q|/r2 are doing.

  1. The formula gives you the size of the field.
  2. So you feed in the magnitude of Q, dropping any minus sign.
  3. The sign of the charge is not thrown away. It tells you the direction, which you decide separately: a field points away from a positive charge and towards a negative one.

Put a negative Q into the arithmetic and you would get a negative field strength, which means nothing. A field has a direction, not a negative size.

Key point

ONE charge makes a field. TWO charges make a force. E = k|Q|/r2 has a single Q in it, the source. F = kq1q2/r2 has two, because a force needs two objects to act between.

Your turn. Test 1 question 8 puts +3 µC and -3 µC 0.10 m apart and asks for the net field at the midpoint. How many charges go into each use of E = k|Q|/r2, and what do you do with the minus sign?

Answer: one charge at a time, and ignore the minus.

Given
Q = 3.0 x 10-6 C from each (magnitudes)
r = 0.05 m to the midpoint
Field from each charge
E = k|Q|/r2
E = (9 x 109 x 3.0 x 10-6) / (0.05)2
E = 27000 / 0.0025
E = 1.08 x 107 N/C
Now the signs, for direction only
away from the positive, towards the negative
at the midpoint both arrows point the SAME way
So they add
E = 2 x 1.08 x 107
Answer
E = 2.16 x 107 N/C

Feed the minus into the arithmetic and they cancel to zero, and zero is one of the wrong answers on offer.

Say it bluntly

Magnitudes go in the formula. Signs decide the direction, afterwards.

blocks.label: Test 1 question 8, worked in full
blocks.problem: Two charges Q1 = +3.0 x 10<sup>-6</sup> C and Q2 = -3.0 x 10<sup>-6</sup> C are placed 0.10 m apart in air. Find the net electric field at the midpoint between the charges.
blocks.working:
Hold this picture in your head first

A positive charge is a FAN. It blows outward, away from itself.
A negative charge is a VACUUM CLEANER. It sucks inward, toward itself.
The electric field is which way the air moves.

Keep that image. It decides this entire question, and you will see why at step 3.

Step 1: Find the distance r from each charge to the midpoint

The charges are 0.10 m apart and you want the field at the midpoint, so you need the distance from each individual charge to that exact middle point. That is half the separation.

r = 0.10 m ÷ 2 = 0.05 m

The same 0.05 m for BOTH charges. Hold on to that, because it is why step 2 only has to be done once.

Step 2: Calculate the SIZE of the field from each charge

The field created by one point charge is:

E = k|Q| / r2

Q1 and Q2 have the same magnitude (3.0 x 10-6 C) and sit at the same distance (0.05 m). So each produces a field of identical size, and one calculation covers both.

  • k = 9 x 109 N m2/C2
  • Q = 3.0 x 10-6 C  (magnitude, so the minus on Q2 is dropped here)
  • r = 0.05 m
E1 = E2 = (9 x 109) x (3.0 x 10-6) ÷ (0.05)2E1 = E2 = 27000 ÷ 0.0025 = 1.08 x 107 N/C

Step 3: Now the direction, and this is what decides the answer

Go back to the picture. On the left is a fan (the positive charge). On the right is a vacuum cleaner (the negative charge). Now stand at the midpoint and ask which way the air moves.

1. The fan on your left blows you to the right.
2. The vacuum on your right sucks you to the right.

Both send you the same way, so the two fields reinforce and add.

Step 4: Add them

Enet = E1 + E2Enet = (1.08 x 107) + (1.08 x 107) = 2.16 x 107 N/C
Carry this into the exam

Fan and vacuum: they cooperate. Two fans: they fight.
A + and a − both push you the same way, so the fields ADD.
Two + charges blow you in opposite directions, so they CANCEL.
Opposite signs add. Same signs cancel. Most people guess that backwards, and the exam offers both answers.
blocks.answer: 2.16 x 10<sup>7</sup> N/C
blocks.redo: Redo it with Q2 changed to +3.0 x 10<sup>-6</sup> C. Now it is TWO FANS, one on each side. The left fan blows you right, the right fan blows you left, and standing in the middle you are pushed equally both ways. The net field is zero. Nothing in the arithmetic changed: both sizes are still 1.08 x 10<sup>7</sup> N/C. Only the picture did.

blocks.label: Which formula does the question want?
blocks.howto: Each frame gives you a question stem. Decide which formula it needs before you slide down.

frames.teach: Read for the QUANTITY asked for and the units offered. Units in N/C or V/m mean a field. Units in volts mean a potential. Units in newtons mean a force.
frames.ask: "A charge of +1.5 x 10<sup>-9</sup> C is placed in a uniform electric field of magnitude 2500 N/C. What is the magnitude of the force?" Which formula?

frames.check: F = qE. The field is GIVEN, so no inverse square is needed at all: F = 1.5 x 10<sup>-9</sup> x 2500 = 3.75 x 10<sup>-6</sup> N. That is Test 1 question 7.
frames.teach: When the field is handed to you, Coulomb's law does not come into it. Students lose this mark by reaching for kQ/r<sup>2</sup> out of habit.
frames.ask: "What is the absolute potential 5 cm from a charge of +4 microcoulombs?" Which formula?

frames.teach: Note that 36000 divided by 0.05 is 720000, not 1800. Dividing by a number less than one makes the answer bigger.
frames.ask: "What is the charge of a system that has 6.2 x 10<sup>18</sup> electrons?" Which formula?

frames.check: q = ne = 6.2 x 10<sup>18</sup> x 1.602 x 10<sup>-19</sup> = 0.99 C. That is Test 1 question 10.
frames.teach: Notice the answer sits just under 1 coulomb. That is because 1/e is about 6.24 x 10<sup>18</sup>, so 6.2 x 10<sup>18</sup> electrons is almost exactly one coulomb. A useful check.
frames.ask: "Calculate the electric field in which an oil drop of mass 8 mg and charge +9 microcoulombs is held stationary." What is the physical condition?

frames.check: Stationary means the forces BALANCE: the electric force up equals the weight down. qE = mg, so E = mg/q.
frames.teach: Now convert: 8 mg is 8 x 10<sup>-6</sup> kg, and 9 microcoulombs is 9 x 10<sup>-6</sup> C. E = (8 x 10<sup>-6</sup> x 10) / (9 x 10<sup>-6</sup>) = 8.89 V/m. The examiner is using g = 10.
frames.ask: Why did the powers of ten vanish so cleanly there?

frames.check: Because 10<sup>-6</sup> appeared on the top and the bottom and cancelled. Spotting that saves the whole calculation.
frames.teach: That is the pattern to look for: when a mass in milligrams meets a charge in microcoulombs, the exponents often cancel.

blocks.label: Your turn
blocks.question: A charge of 8 x 10-8 C sits 0.40 m from a charge of -2.0 x 10-8 C. Determine the electric field produced by the NEGATIVE charge at the location of the positive charge.
blocks.answer:
Only the negative charge produces the field being asked about, so only it goes into the formula.

Given
Q = 2.0 x 10-8 C (magnitude)
r = 0.40 m
k = 9 x 109

Formula
E = k|Q|/r2

Substitute
E = (9 x 109 x 2.0 x 10-8) / (0.40)2
E = 180 / 0.16

Answer
E = 1125 N/C

The 8 x 10-8 C charge is where you are standing. Using it instead gives about four times the answer, which is one of the offered options. Test 1 question 13.

blocks.sub: Magnitudes go in the formula, signs decide the direction.

kick: The other half of Part B
title: Potential, Energy and the Uniform Field
lead: Potential is the twin of the field, and the exam separates them with one difference: the field is squared and the potential is not. Getting that straight is worth marks on both tests.

blocks.label: The hill
blocks.html:
Start with a hill. Standing on it, two different things can be asked about where you are.

  1. How high are you? That is a single number. No direction. Just a height.
  2. How steep is it here? That has a direction: the slope points down some particular way.

Electric potential is the height. Electric field is the steepness. They are two descriptions of the same hill, and every question is asking for one or the other.

Potential VField E
Hill wordHeightSteepness
FormulaV = kQ/rE = k|Q|/r2
Vector or scalarScalar, just a numberVector, it has a direction
Unitvolt, VN/C, the same as V/m
Key point, and the exam lives here

E = kQ/r2 but V = kQ/r.
The field is squared. The potential is not.
Why? Because the field is a vector spreading over a sphere, and the potential is the total climb, which thins out more slowly.

Your turn. You move from 5 cm to 20 cm away from a charge, four times further out. What happens to the field, and what happens to the potential?

Field: 1 over 4 squared = a SIXTEENTH
E = kQ/r2, so 4 becomes 16

Potential: 1 over 4 = a QUARTER
V = kQ/r, so 4 stays 4

Check it on the real paper
Test 1 question 4 goes 5 cm to 20 cm
720 kV falls to 180 kV
720/180 = 4, a quarter

Had you squared it you would have hunted for a sixteenth and found no such option.

Say it bluntly

Field squared, potential plain. Say it every time you see an r.

blocks.label: The potential formulas
blocks.html:
QuantityFormulaNote
Potential of a point chargeV = kQ/rScalar, and the r is PLAIN
Potential energyU = kQq/r = qVIn joules
Work done moving a chargeW = qVCharge times voltage
Field from potentialE = -dV/dr, and E = V/d if uniformThe uniform form is the one the exam uses

What every letter means

SymbolMeaningUnit
VElectric potential, the energy each coulomb would have at that pointvolt, V, which IS a joule per coulomb
QThe charge PRODUCING the potentialcoulomb, C
qThe charge you are MOVING or placing therecoulomb, C
UPotential energy of that charge at that placejoule, J
WWork done moving the charge through the potential differencejoule, J
rDistance from the source charge, in metres, NOT squared heremetre, m
dGap between two parallel plates, in metresmetre, m
Why W = qV is almost a definition

A volt IS a joule per coulomb. So coulombs times volts gives joules, and W = qV is really just the unit written as an equation. Once you see that, you never have to memorise it.

Note the sign in V = kQ/r. Unlike the field formula, there are no magnitude bars here. Potential is a scalar, so a negative charge really does produce a negative potential, and you keep the minus.

blocks.label: The uniform field between plates
blocks.tag: the other kind of field question
blocks.html:
Everything so far has been the field of a point charge, which weakens as you move away. Between two parallel plates something different happens: the field is the same everywhere in the gap.

E = V/d (E the uniform field in V/m, V the voltage across the plates, d the gap between them in METRES)

Key point

No r, no squaring, no k. A uniform field question is a division, and the only work in it is converting the gap to metres.

Your turn. Two plates 2 mm apart have 60 V across them. What is the field?

Convert first
2 mm = 0.002 m
Formula
E = V/d
Substitute
E = 60 / 0.002
Answer
E = 30000 V/m

Leave the gap in millimetres and you get 30 V/m, wrong by a factor of a thousand.

Look at the size of that answer. A modest 60 V across a gap you can barely see produces thirty thousand volts per metre. That is exactly why capacitors are built with their plates as close together as possible, and also why they eventually break down: push the field high enough and even the insulator between them gives way.

blocks.label: Equipotentials, and why no work is done along them
blocks.html:
Start back on the hill. Walk around it at a constant height, following a contour line on a map. You go a long way, but you never climb.

An equipotential is exactly that contour: a surface on which the potential is the same everywhere.

Key point

W = qV depends on the CHANGE in potential. Along an equipotential there is no change, so no work is done, no matter how far you travel.

One consequence follows immediately, and examiners like it: field lines always cross an equipotential at right angles. If a field line had any component ALONG the surface, it would push a charge along it and do work, which would mean the potential changed. It did not. So the field can only point straight across.

The everyday case: around a point charge the equipotentials are spheres, one inside another like the layers of an onion. Move around a sphere and you do nothing. Move outward from one sphere to the next and you have climbed.

Your turn. How much work is done carrying a 5 C charge right around a circle centred on a point charge?

Zero.

The circle is an equipotential
so V at the end = V at the start
so the CHANGE in V is 0
W = qV = 5 x 0
W = 0 J

The 5 C was never needed. Any charge, any size of circle, still zero.

blocks.label: Test 1 question 4, worked in full
blocks.problem: A charge of +4 µC is in air. Find the absolute potential at 5 cm from it, and then at 20 cm from it.
blocks.working:
Step 1: Convert both distances before anything else

  • 5 cm = 0.05 m
  • 20 cm = 0.20 m
  • Q = 4 µC = 4 x 10-6 C
  • k = 9 x 109 N m2/C2

Step 2: Choose the formula, and notice the r is plain

V = kQ / r   (not r squared, this is the potential)

Step 3: The first distance

V = (9 x 109 x 4 x 10-6) ÷ 0.05V = 36000 ÷ 0.05 = 720000 V = 720 kV

Dividing by 0.05 MULTIPLIES by 20. If your answer came out smaller than 36000, you divided the wrong way round.

Step 4: The second distance

V = 36000 ÷ 0.20 = 180000 V = 180 kV

Step 5: Check the ratio, which is the real lesson

720 ÷ 180 = 4

The distance went up 4 times and the potential fell to a QUARTER, not a sixteenth. That is V = kQ/r with its plain r, visible in the numbers.
blocks.answer: 720 kV at 5 cm, and 180 kV at 20 cm
blocks.redo: Redo it as a FIELD question, E = k|Q|/r<sup>2</sup>, at the same two distances. You get 1.44 x 10<sup>7</sup> N/C and 9.0 x 10<sup>5</sup> N/C, a ratio of 16. Same charge, same distances, and the ratio is squared. That contrast is the whole of this lesson in two lines.

blocks.label: Your turn
blocks.question:
(1) How much work is done moving 3 C through a potential difference of 12 V?

(2) A charge sits at a point where the potential is 500 V. Its charge is 2 µC. What is its potential energy?

(3) Two plates 5 mm apart carry a uniform field of 4000 V/m. What is the voltage across them?
blocks.answer:
(1) W = qV = 3 x 12 = 36 J. Coulombs times volts gives joules, because a volt is a joule per coulomb.

(2) U = qV = 2 x 10-6 x 500 = 1 x 10-3 J, that is 1 mJ.

(3) Rearrange E = V/d to V = Ed. Convert first: 5 mm = 0.005 m. V = 4000 x 0.005 = 20 V. Here you MULTIPLY by the small number, so the answer is small. Dividing instead gives 800000, which is the slip to watch for.

blocks.tag: topic 2, as the examiner set it

blocks.big: Field is squared, potential is not
blocks.sub: And no work is ever done along an equipotential.

title: Flux, Gauss, Lines, Sheets and Conductors
lead: Flux questions are among the easiest on the paper if you know where the angle is measured from, and Gauss turns a sphere into a point charge in one line.

blocks.text: Flux is just how much field goes through

blocks.label: The rain and the hoop
blocks.html:
Start with rain. Hold a hoop out in falling rain.

  1. Face the hoop straight up and the most rain falls through it.
  2. Tilt it, and less gets through.
  3. Turn it edge on to the rain, and none does.

Nothing about the rain changed. Only the angle of the hoop did. Flux is exactly that idea: how much field passes through a surface.

Φ = EA cos θ (Φ the flux in N m2/C, E the field in N/C, A the area of the surface in m2, θ the angle measured from the NORMAL)

Key point

The angle is measured from the normal, the line sticking straight out of the surface. NOT from the surface itself. Get that backwards and every flux answer inverts.

Your turn. The hoop faces the rain squarely. What is θ, and what is cos θ?

Answer: θ = 0, and cos 0 = 1.

Squarely on means the field goes straight through, so the angle from the NORMAL is zero, not ninety.

Flux, squarely on
Φ = EA cos 0
Φ = EA x 1
= the maximum

Flux, edge on
Φ = EA cos 90
Φ = EA x 0
= 0, nothing gets through

And edge on? θ = 90 degrees, cos 90 = 0, and nothing gets through at all.

Say it bluntly

Straight through is zero degrees, not ninety.

blocks.label: Test 1 question 5
blocks.problem: A uniform electric field E = 200 N/C passes through a surface of area 2 m<sup>2</sup> at 0 degrees. Find the flux.
blocks.working:
Given
E = 200 N/C
A = 2 m2
θ = 0 degrees

Formula
Φ = EA cos θ

Substitute
Φ = 200 x 2 x cos 0
  = 200 x 2 x 1
  = 400
blocks.answer: 400 N m<sup>2</sup>/C
blocks.redo: Redo it at 60 degrees. cos 60 = 0.5, so the flux halves to 200. Redo it at 90 degrees and it is zero, because the field never crosses the surface at all.

blocks.label: Gauss in one sentence
blocks.html:
Φ = Qenclosed / ε0. Flux out equals charge in, divided by ε0.

SymbolMeaningUnit
ΦTotal flux out through the whole closed surfaceN m2/C
QenclosedThe charge INSIDE the surface. Nothing else countscoulomb, C
ε0Permittivity of free space8.85 x 10-12 F m-1

Three consequences the paper uses:

  • A charge OUTSIDE the surface contributes nothing. Every field line it sends in comes back out, so the ins and the outs cancel exactly.
  • Outside a charged sphere, the field is the same as if all the charge sat at the centre. So E = kQ/r2 with r measured from the centre.
  • Inside a hollow conductor the field is zero, because no charge is enclosed. That is the Faraday cage.
The hook

Gauss only counts what is inside the bag. Whatever is outside can shine straight through it, in one side and out the other, and contribute nothing at all.

blocks.label: The Gaussian surface is imaginary
blocks.tag: a definition the exam asks for
blocks.html:
Gauss's law mentions a closed surface. It is worth being very clear about what that surface is.

Key point

A Gaussian surface is an imaginary closed surface that you draw on the diagram, chosen to make the law easy. Nothing is built. Nothing is placed. It is a line on paper.

Because you choose it, you choose it to suit the symmetry:

Charge arrangementSurface you drawWhy
Point charge, or a sphereA sphere around itE is the same size everywhere on it
Long straight line of chargeA cylinder around the lineE is the same all round the curved side
Flat sheet of chargeA box through the sheetE is the same on the two flat faces

In each case the point is the same: pick a surface on which E is constant, and the integral collapses to E times an area.

You will meet its twin in magnetism. The Amperian loop in Ampere's law is the identical idea: an imaginary path, chosen for convenience, that turns a hard integral into a multiplication. Same trick, different field.

blocks.label: The three standard fields, and how fast each falls off
blocks.html:
Gauss gives three results the exam expects you to recognise on sight. The pattern is what to learn, not the algebra.

Charge shapeFieldFalls off as
Point chargeE = kQ/r21/r2
Infinite LINE chargeE = λ/(2πε0r)1/r
Infinite PLANE sheetE = σ/(2ε0)Not at all

What the two new letters mean

SymbolMeaningUnit
λCharge per unit LENGTH along the lineC/m
σCharge per unit AREA on the sheetC/m2
rDistance from the line, and note it is NOT squaredmetre, m
Why the pattern makes sense

It is all about how the field has to spread.
A point spreads over a growing SPHERE, area 4πr2, so the field thins as 1/r2.
A line spreads over a growing CYLINDER, area 2πrL, which grows only with r, so the field thins as 1/r.
A plane does not spread at all, so the field never thins. Look at the formula: there is no r in it anywhere.

The plane result is genuinely surprising, so test it. Stand 1 cm from an infinite charged sheet, then walk back 10 m. The field is identical. That is what makes the uniform field between capacitor plates possible, and it is why E = V/d has no distance-from-the-plate in it.

One more link worth carrying forward: a straight current-carrying wire also falls as 1/r, for exactly the same cylindrical reason. Same geometry, different field.

blocks.label: Why the field inside a conductor is zero
blocks.html:
Start with the lightning and the car. A car is struck by lightning and the people inside are unharmed. It is not the tyres. It is the metal.

Here is the argument, in four steps.

  1. In a conductor, charge moves freely.
  2. So any excess charge pushes itself apart until it reaches the outer surface, as far from the rest as it can get.
  3. Draw a Gaussian surface just inside the metal. It encloses no charge at all.
  4. Gauss then forces Φ = 0, and so E = 0 everywhere inside.
Key point

E = 0 inside a conductor, and it is not a separate rule to memorise. It is Gauss's law plus the fact that charge on a conductor lives on the outside.

The everyday cases: a car in a lightning storm, a microwave oven's mesh door keeping the microwaves in, a metal cabinet screening sensitive electronics, and the metal-lined bag that protects a computer part in the post. All the same effect, and it has a name: the Faraday cage.

Your turn. A hollow copper sphere sits in a very strong external field. What is the field at its centre?

Zero.

Charge rearranges on the outer surface
until the inside field cancels exactly
no enclosed charge
so no flux
so no field

The strength of the external field does not matter. Stronger field, more rearrangement, still zero inside.

blocks.label: From the centre, not the surface
blocks.html:
"A conducting sphere of radius 0.25 m carries 6 x 10-6 C. Find the field at a point 0.50 m from the centre."

The radius is there for one reason only: to tell you 0.50 m is OUTSIDE the sphere, so the point-charge result applies. It does not enter the arithmetic.

E = 9 x 109 x 6 x 10-6 / (0.50)2 = 54000 / 0.25 = 2.16 x 105 N/C.

Adding the radius to the distance, or subtracting it, both produce offered options. Read whether the distance is from the centre or from the surface.

blocks.label: Your turn
blocks.question:
(1) A closed surface encloses 3 µC. A further 10 µC sits just outside it. What is the net flux through the surface?

(2) What is the electric field deep inside a solid copper block sitting in a strong external field?

(3) You double your distance from an infinite line charge. What happens to the field?

(4) You double your distance from an infinite charged sheet. What happens to the field?
blocks.answer:
(1) Only the enclosed charge counts.

Given
Q enclosed = 3 x 10-6 C
Q outside = 10 x 10-6 C, which contributes NOTHING
ε0 = 8.85 x 10-12

Formula
Φ = Qenclosed / ε0

Substitute
Φ = 3 x 10-6 / 8.85 x 10-12

Answer
Φ = 3.39 x 105 N m2/C

(2) Zero. Charge rearranges on the surface until the interior field cancels exactly. No enclosed charge, no field. That is the Faraday cage.

(3) It HALVES. A line falls as 1/r, so double the distance is half the field, not a quarter.

(4) Nothing at all. E = σ/(2ε0) has no r in it. Distance from an infinite sheet does not enter.

blocks.sub: Point falls as 1 over r squared, line as 1 over r, sheet not at all.

title: Capacitance, Geometry and Dielectrics
lead: Capacitance came up four times on Test 1. The whole topic rests on one sentence that almost everybody gets wrong at first: charging a capacitor harder does not change its capacitance.

blocks.label: The bucket
blocks.html:
Start with a bucket. A capacitor stores charge, and capacitance is simply how wide the bucket is: how much charge it holds for each volt you apply.

C = Q/V. Charge per volt. (C the capacitance in farads, Q the charge stored in coulombs, V the voltage across it in volts)

One farad is one coulomb per volt. That is the definition of the unit, and it is the formula read aloud.

Now here is the part that catches almost everybody.

  1. Raise the voltage, and you push more charge in.
  2. But the charge rises in exact proportion to the voltage.
  3. So the RATIO does not move. Q went up, V went up, Q/V is unchanged.
Key point

You cannot widen a bucket by pouring more into it. Capacitance is fixed by GEOMETRY: the plate area, the gap, and what sits in the gap.

Look at the parallel-plate formula and you can see it directly:

C = εrε0A/d (A the plate area, d the gap between the plates, εr how many times better than vacuum the filling is)

Your turn. Find Q in that formula. Find V.

Answer: neither is there.

Look at the formula
C = εrε0A/d
The symbols in it
εr = the filling
ε0 = a constant
A = plate area
d = the gap
Charge Q? absent
Voltage V? absent

Not one symbol is a charge or a voltage. That is why a question can give you a capacitor's dimensions and nothing else and still expect an answer.

Say it bluntly

Charging it harder does not change its capacitance.

blocks.label: The capacitance formulas
blocks.html:
QuantityFormulaNote
DefinitionC = Q/VUnit farad, one coulomb per volt
Parallel plateC = εrε0A/dNo Q and no V in it
Isolated sphereC = 4πε0RRadius alone, and no second plate

What every letter means

SymbolMeaningUnit
CCapacitance, the charge stored per volt appliedfarad, F
QCharge stored on one platecoulomb, C
VVoltage across the capacitorvolt, V
AArea of ONE plate, the overlap between themsquare metre, m2
dGap between the plates, that is the dielectric thicknessmetre, m
RRadius of the isolated spheremetre, m
ε0Permittivity of free space8.85 x 10-12 F m-1
εrRelative permittivity of the dielectric, how many times better than vacuumnone, it is a ratio. 1 in vacuum
The sphere is the cleanest proof of the point

C = 4πε0R. Nothing but a radius and two constants. No charge, no voltage, no second plate. A bigger ball is a bigger bucket, and that is the entire story.

Watch the two Cs. Italic C is capacitance, upright C is the coulomb. And εr has no unit at all: it just says how many times the dielectric beats a vacuum, so 7 means seven times the capacitance.

blocks.label: Permittivity, permeability, and the dielectric
blocks.html:
Two similar-looking words run through the whole course, and mixing them up costs marks in both halves of it.

WordSymbolWhat it measuresBelongs to
PermittivityεHow readily a material permits an electric fieldCapacitors, Gauss, Coulomb
PermeabilityµHow readily a material permits a magnetic fieldSolenoids, wires, Ampere
The hook

ε sounds like Electric. µ goes with Magnetic.
Both words start with permit, because both are asking the same question of a material: how easily do you let this field through?

Now the dielectric, which is where permittivity earns its keep.

  1. A dielectric is simply an insulator placed between the plates: mica, glass, waxed paper, plastic film.
  2. Putting one in always increases the capacitance.
  3. By how much? By the factor εr, so C = εr C0 where C0 was the capacitance with vacuum in the gap.

Your turn. A capacitor of 3 µF in vacuum is filled with a material of εr = 5. What is its capacitance now?

Formula
C = εr C0
Substitute
C = 5 x 3
Answer
C = 15 µF

Always bigger, never smaller. εr is 1 for vacuum and never less than 1 for anything else, so an answer below 3 µF would be impossible.

blocks.label: Why a dielectric helps at all: polarisation
blocks.html:
It is worth knowing WHY stuffing an insulator into the gap helps, because the exam asks for the word.

  1. The atoms of the insulator have positive nuclei and negative electron clouds, normally sitting on top of each other.
  2. Switch on the field and each atom stretches very slightly: the positive shifts one way, the negative the other.
  3. Each atom has become a tiny dipole, a pair of equal and opposite charges a small distance apart.
  4. These induced dipoles line up and produce a field opposing the original one, which lowers the voltage across the plates.
  5. Lower V for the same Q means, by C = Q/V, a larger C.
Polarisation

Polarisation is the creation of induced dipoles in an insulator by an applied field. That is the definition, and the chain above is why a dielectric always increases capacitance rather than decreasing it.

The everyday case: rub a balloon on your hair and hold it near a thin stream of water from a tap. The stream bends towards the balloon, although water is neutral overall. The balloon's field polarised the water molecules, and the near end of each is now attracted. Same physics, visible in a kitchen.

blocks.label: Three capacitance questions from Test 1
blocks.howto: Work each step before sliding down to the answer.

frames.teach: Test 1 question 6 gives a parallel plate: area 4 x 10<sup>-2</sup> m<sup>2</sup>, dielectric thickness 10<sup>-3</sup> m, relative permittivity 7. The formula is C = epsilon-r epsilon-0 A / d.
A capacitance in nanofarads is believable. Two of the offered options have POSITIVE exponents, which would be a capacitor larger than any ever built. Step 7 kills them instantly.
frames.ask: Test 1 question 11: a sphere carries 4.5 nC at 180 V above its surroundings. Find its capacitance.

frames.teach: All the talk of spheres and insulating rods is scenery. The moment you see a charge and a voltage, C = Q/V is the whole question.
frames.ask: That sphere: could you have found its capacitance from its RADIUS instead, without knowing the charge or the voltage?

frames.check: Yes. C = 4 pi epsilon-nought R for an isolated sphere. Radius alone is enough, which is the clearest proof that capacitance is geometry.
frames.teach: Two routes to the same number, one through charge and voltage and one through pure geometry. If a question gives you a radius and no charge, that is the route it wants.

blocks.label: Your turn
blocks.question:
(1) A capacitor holds 12 µC at 4 V. What is its capacitance?

(2) You double the plate SEPARATION of a parallel-plate capacitor. What happens to C?

(3) What is the difference between permittivity and permeability?
blocks.answer:
(1) C = Q/V = 12 x 10-6 / 4 = 3 x 10-6 F, that is 3 µF.

(2) It HALVES. C = εrε0A/d, and d is on the bottom, so doubling it halves C. Plates close together mean a bigger capacitor, which is why real capacitors are rolled up tightly.

(3) Permittivity ε is how readily a material permits an ELECTRIC field. Permeability µ is how readily it permits a MAGNETIC field. ε for electric, µ for magnetic.

blocks.sub: Charging it harder changes Q and V together, never C.

title: Capacitor Networks, Stored Energy and Dipoles
lead: The networks are where the marks are, and reading the picture matters more than the formula. Then the energy formula, and the dipole that keeps reappearing all the way into magnetism.

blocks.text: Series and parallel, and why capacitors are backwards

blocks.label: Wider bucket or deeper stack
blocks.html:
Two capacitors can be joined in two ways, and the results feel the wrong way round until you see why.

ArrangementFormulaResult
Parallel, side by side across the same two pointsC = C1 + C2They simply ADD
Series, one after the other in the same branch1/C = 1/C1 + 1/C2LESS than the smallest

Why parallel adds. Two capacitors side by side are just one bigger pair of plates. More plate area means a wider bucket, and area adds.

Why series shrinks. One after the other, the gaps add up, and d is on the BOTTOM of C = εrε0A/d. A bigger total gap means a smaller capacitance.

Key point, and it is the trap of the topic

Capacitors are backwards from resistors.
Capacitors ADD in parallel.
Resistors ADD in series.
Learn ONE of them properly and flip it for the other. Trying to hold both separately is how people end up guessing.

Your turn. 2 µF and 3 µF in series. Before calculating: must the answer be above 3, between 2 and 3, or below 2?

Below 2.

Series always gives less than the SMALLEST

Check it
1/C = 1/2 + 1/3
= 3/6 + 2/6 = 5/6
C = 6/5 = 1.2 µF

1.2 is below 2. If your series answer ever comes out bigger than the smallest capacitor, you forgot to flip the reciprocal back.

blocks.label: Test 1 question 2, the network with the figure
blocks.problem: C1 = 1 µF and C2 = 5 µF sit one above the other in the same branch. That branch spans the same two terminals as C3 = 8 µF. Find the total capacitance.
blocks.working:
Step 1: read the arrangement, before any formula.
C1 and C2 are in the SAME branch, one after the other, so the same charge must pass through both: they are in series.
That branch and C3 span the same two terminals, so they are in parallel.

Step 2: series first.
1/Cs = 1/1 + 1/5
  = 5/5 + 1/5
  = 6/5
Cs = 5/6 = 0.833 µF

Note the flip back at the end. 6/5 was 1/C, so C is 5/6. Forgetting to invert is the commonest slip in the whole topic.

Step 3: then parallel, which simply adds.
C = 0.833 + 8
  = 8.83 µF

Step 4: check.
Adding anything in parallel can only INCREASE the total, so the answer had to be above 8. It is. And the series pair came out below 1, the smaller of the two, as it had to.
blocks.answer: 8.8 µF
blocks.redo: Two wrong answers are offered as traps: 0.8 µF is the series step with C3 forgotten, and 14.0 µF is all three added as though everything were parallel. Redo the problem with all three in series and confirm you get less than 1 µF, which is the sanity check for series.

blocks.label: The energy stored
blocks.html:
W = ½CV2 = ½QV = Q2/2C, three forms of the same thing.

SymbolMeaningUnit
WEnergy stored in the capacitorjoule, J
CCapacitancefarad, F
VVoltage it is charged to. In the first form it is SQUAREDvolt, V
QCharge storedcoulomb, C

Which form to use: whichever two quantities the question gives you. C and V, use ½CV2. Q and V, use ½QV. Q and C, use Q2/2C. They always agree.

Where the half comes from

The voltage climbed from zero as the capacitor charged. The first drop of charge crossed almost no potential difference, the last crossed the full V, so on average each crossed V/2.

That is why it is ½QV and not QV. And you will meet the identical argument again in ½LI2 for an inductor, where the CURRENT climbed from zero.

The everyday case: a camera flash. A capacitor charges slowly from a small battery over a second or two, then dumps all of that stored W in about a thousandth of a second. The energy was never large; the POWER is, because power is energy divided by time.

blocks.label: The dipole
blocks.html:
You met induced dipoles in the last lesson. Here is the object itself, because the exam defines it and then uses it twice more.

Definition

A dipole is two equal and opposite charges separated by a small distance. Plus q at one end, minus q at the other, a distance d apart.

Three formulas go with it, and they follow one after the other.

QuantityFormulaMeaning of the letters
Dipole momentp = qdq the size of ONE charge in C, d the separation in m, p in C m
Torque in a fieldτ = pE sin θE the external field, θ the angle between the dipole and the field, τ in N m
Energy in a fieldU = -pE cos θSame letters, U in joules

Read the two angle formulas together and they tell one story.

  1. At θ = 0, lined up with the field: sin 0 = 0, so no torque. And cos 0 = 1, so U = -pE, the lowest energy. Nothing turns it, and it sits happily.
  2. At θ = 90, across the field: sin 90 = 1, so the torque is at its maximum. The field twists it hard.
  3. At θ = 180, pointing backwards: sin 180 = 0 again, so no torque, but cos 180 = -1 gives U = +pE, the highest energy. Balanced, but ready to flip at the slightest nudge.
The everyday case, and the memory hook

A compass needle. Held across north it feels a strong twist. Released, it swings to north and stops. Once aligned it feels no twist at all and sits at its lowest energy.

Every dipole in this course does exactly that. And when you meet the magnetic dipole τ = mB sin θ in Part E, it is the same sentence with m in place of p and B in place of E.

Your turn. Charges of plus and minus 2 nC sit 3 mm apart. What is the dipole moment?

Convert first
q = 2 x 10-9 C
d = 3 x 10-3 m
Formula
p = qd
Substitute
p = 2 x 10-9 x 3 x 10-3
Answer
p = 6 x 10-12 C m

Use ONE of the charges, not both, and not their sum. The pair is what makes it a dipole; q is the size of either one.

blocks.label: The energy question, and the half
blocks.howto: Work each step before sliding down.

frames.teach: Test 1 question 15: a capacitor stores 2.25 mJ when charged to 30 V. Find C. Start by rearranging W = half C V squared in symbols.
frames.ask: Rearrange it for C, then substitute.

frames.check: C = 2W/V<sup>2</sup> = (2 x 2.25 x 10<sup>-3</sup>) / 900 = 4.5 x 10<sup>-3</sup> / 900 = 5 x 10<sup>-6</sup> F = 5 microfarads.
frames.teach: Two things to get right: the factor of 2 when you rearrange, and squaring the 30 to 900. Forgetting the half gives 2.5 microfarads, which is an offered option.
frames.ask: Same capacitor, same 30 V. How much CHARGE is on it?

frames.check: Q = CV = 5 x 10<sup>-6</sup> x 30 = 1.5 x 10<sup>-4</sup> C. Then check with the other energy form: half QV = 0.5 x 1.5 x 10<sup>-4</sup> x 30 = 2.25 x 10<sup>-3</sup> J, which is the 2.25 mJ we started from.
frames.teach: The three energy forms agreeing is a free check on any capacitor answer. If they disagree, one of your numbers is wrong.
frames.ask: Why is there a half in the energy formula at all?

frames.check: Because the voltage climbed from zero as the capacitor charged. The first charge crossed almost no potential difference, the last crossed the full V, so the average was V/2.
frames.teach: The same argument produces the half in half L I squared for an inductor, which you will meet in the induction lesson.

blocks.label: Your turn
blocks.question:
(1) 4 µF and 12 µF in parallel. Find the total.

(2) The same two in series. Find the total, and check it against the sanity rule.

(3) A dipole sits at 90 degrees to a field. Is the torque a maximum or a minimum, and is it stable?
blocks.answer:
(1) Parallel simply adds: 4 + 12 = 16 µF. Bigger than either, as parallel always is.

(2) 1/C = 1/4 + 1/12 = 3/12 + 1/12 = 4/12, so C = 12/4 = 3 µF. Below 4, the smaller of the two, so the sanity check holds. Note the flip back at the end.

(3) Maximum torque, since sin 90 = 1, and it is not stable at all: the field is twisting it hard towards alignment. The stable position is at 0 degrees, lined up, where the torque is zero and the energy is lowest.

kick: The vocabulary of every circuit question
title: Current, Ohm's Law, Resistivity and Materials
lead: Before any network can be solved, four words have to be exact: current, resistance, resistivity and ohmic. The exam asks for the definitions directly, and then uses them in every calculation.

blocks.text: Current is a rate, not an amount

blocks.label: Water through a pipe
blocks.html:
Start with a tap. Ask two different questions. How much water came out? That is litres. How fast is it flowing? That is litres per second.

Charge and current are that same pair.

Charge QCurrent I
Water wordLitresLitres per second
It is aTotal amountRate
Unitcoulomb, Campere, A

I = ΔQ / Δt (I the current in amperes, ΔQ the charge that passed in coulombs, Δt the time it took in seconds)

Key point, and it is the unit written out

One ampere is one coulomb per second.
So the ampere is not a new idea at all. It is the coulomb, per second, exactly as the formula says.

The battery's side of the story is the energy it hands each coulomb:

W = ΔQ × ε (W the work done in joules, ΔQ the charge pushed round in coulombs, ε the emf in volts)

Which is W = qV wearing a battery's clothes. A volt is a joule per coulomb, so coulombs times volts is joules, every time.

Your turn. 60 C passes a point in 20 seconds. What is the current? And how much work did a 12 V battery do pushing it?

Current
I = ΔQ/Δt
I = 60/20
I = 3 A

Work
W = ΔQ × ε
W = 60 x 12
W = 720 J

Notice the current did not enter the second one. The work depends on how much charge went round, not how quickly.

blocks.label: Ohm's law and the ohm
blocks.html:
V = IR

SymbolMeaningUnit
VVoltage, or potential difference, ACROSS the componentvolt, V
ICurrent THROUGH the componentampere, A
RResistance of the componentohm, Ω
The rearrangement trick

Write V on top, with I and R side by side underneath.
Cover the one you want and the formula reads itself:
cover V, and you see I times R
cover I, and you see V over R
cover R, and you see V over I

You never have to do algebra on V = IR again.

The ohm, defined: one ohm is one volt per amp. Read straight off R = V/I, exactly as the ampere read off I = Q/t.

And the word ohmic: a component is ohmic if it obeys Ohm's law, meaning its resistance stays constant as the voltage changes, at a fixed temperature. Double the voltage, double the current, and R does not budge. A filament lamp is NOT ohmic, because it heats up and its resistance climbs.

blocks.label: Resistivity: long and thin resists
blocks.html:
Resistance is not just a property of a material. It depends on the SHAPE of the piece you cut.

R = ρL/A

SymbolMeaningUnit
RResistance of this particular pieceohm, Ω
ρResistivity, the material's own intrinsic opposition to currentohm metre, Ω m
LLength of the piece, along the currentmetre, m
ACross-sectional area, the face the current passes throughsquare metre, m2
The hook, four words

Long and thin resists. Short and fat does not.
L is on top, so LONGER means more resistance.
A is on the bottom, so THINNER means more resistance.

The everyday case: a garden hose. A long narrow hose gives you a trickle. A short wide one gives you a torrent. Same water pressure, same tap, different pipe.

Resistivity against resistance, and the exam does ask.

Resistivity ρResistance R
Belongs toThe MATERIALThe PIECE you cut
Changes if youChange copper for ironCut it longer or thinner
Unitohm metreohm

Your turn. You replace a wire with one of the same material, twice as long and twice the cross-sectional area. What happens to its resistance?

Nothing. It is unchanged.

R = ρL/A
L doubles: R would double
A doubles: R would halve
2 x ½ = 1

The two changes cancel exactly. That is why you must read BOTH dimensions before answering.

blocks.label: Three words the exam defines directly
blocks.tag: easy marks if you have the words
blocks.html:
Three definitions that appear as fill-in-the-gap and true-or-false questions, where knowing the exact wording is the entire mark.

WordDefinitionThe detail that is marked
SemiconductorA material between a conductor and an insulatorIts resistance FALLS as it heats, which is backwards from a metal
DopingAdding impurities to a semiconductor to make it conductDeliberate contamination, not a defect
Short circuitA path of zero resistanceIt carries all the current, so everything in parallel with it is bypassed
Why a semiconductor is backwards

Heat a metal and its atoms vibrate harder, getting in the way of the moving charge, so resistance rises.
Heat a semiconductor and the extra energy frees more charge carriers than it obstructs, so resistance falls.

Same heat, opposite result. That contrast is exactly what the exam tests.

The everyday case for a short circuit: a bare wire falls across the two terminals of a battery. Current takes the zero-resistance path in preference to everything else, rises enormously since I = V/R with R near zero, and the wire gets hot enough to burn. That is what a fuse exists to interrupt.

Your turn. A 10 Ω lamp has a short circuit placed directly across it. How much current now flows through the lamp?

Essentially none.

The short is 0 Ω, the lamp is 10 Ω
they are in parallel
current takes the path of least resistance
so it all goes through the short

The lamp goes out although it is undamaged and still connected. Examiners like this one because nothing about the lamp changed.

blocks.label: Your turn
blocks.question:
(1) Define the ampere.

(2) Define the ohm.

(3) What does ohmic mean?

(4) A wire is stretched to three times its length, the material and volume unchanged so its area falls to a third. What happens to R?

(5) 240 V across a 60 Ω heater. Find the current.
blocks.answer:
(1) One ampere is one coulomb per second.

(2) One ohm is one volt per amp.

(3) Obeying Ohm's law: the resistance stays constant as the voltage changes, at a fixed temperature.

(4) R = ρL/A. L triples, so R triples. A falls to a third, so R triples again. Total: nine times the original resistance. Stretching a wire raises its resistance far faster than people expect.

(5) I = V/R = 240/60 = 4 A.

title: Resistor Networks, Dividers and Kirchhoff's Laws
lead: Two laws, two network rules and two dividers. Between them they solve every circuit the paper can set, and each one has a free check built into it.

blocks.text: Series and parallel, with their sanity checks

blocks.label: One road or two
blocks.html:
Start with traffic. Two roadworks one after the other on the same road: you are held up twice, so the total delay adds. Now open a second road alongside: traffic splits and everyone gets through faster than on either road alone.

Resistors do exactly that.

ArrangementFormulaSanity check
Series, one after the otherR = R1 + R2Bigger than either. Same current through both
Parallel, side by side1/R = 1/R1 + 1/R2Less than the smallest. Same voltage across both
Two in parallel onlyR = R1R2/(R1+R2)Product over sum. Faster for exactly two
The free check, worth using every time

A parallel total is ALWAYS less than the smallest resistor in it.
If your answer is bigger, you almost certainly forgot to flip 1/R back into R at the end. That one check catches the most common circuit slip there is.

And remember the flip from capacitors. Resistors add in SERIES. Capacitors add in PARALLEL. Learn one properly, flip it for the other.

Your turn. 6 Ω and 3 Ω in parallel. Use product over sum, then check it.

Product over sum
R = (6 x 3)/(6 + 3)
R = 18/9
R = 2 Ω

Check
2 is less than 3, the smallest
so it passes

Had you added them to 9 Ω, the check would have failed instantly.

blocks.label: The two dividers
blocks.tag: one has the OTHER resistor on top
blocks.html:
When two resistors share a voltage or a current, you can get either share in one line, without solving the whole circuit.

DividerFormulaWhat is on top
Voltage divider, resistors in seriesV1 = (R1/Rtotal) x VThe resistor you WANT the voltage across
Current divider, resistors in parallelI1 = (R2/(R1+R2)) x ItotalThe OTHER resistor
Why one of them is swapped, and this is the whole trick

Voltage goes where the resistance is. A bigger resistor takes a bigger share of the voltage, so its own R sits on top.
Current avoids resistance. A bigger resistor takes a SMALLER share of the current, so the OTHER resistor sits on top.

Say it as: voltage prefers the big one, current prefers the small one.

Your turn. 4 Ω and 6 Ω in series across 20 V. What is the voltage across the 6 Ω?

Formula
V6 = (R6/Rtotal) x V
Substitute
V6 = (6/10) x 20
Answer
V6 = 12 V

Check
the 4 Ω must take the other 8 V
12 + 8 = 20, the full supply

And the bigger resistor took the bigger share, exactly as voltage should.

Now the current divider, with the same two resistors in PARALLEL across a 5 A supply. How much goes through the 6 Ω?

Formula, OTHER resistor on top
I6 = (R4/(R4+R6)) x I
Substitute
I6 = (4/10) x 5
Answer
I6 = 2 A

Check
the 4 Ω takes the other 3 A
2 + 3 = 5, the full current

And the SMALLER resistor took the bigger current, exactly as it should.

blocks.label: Kirchhoff's two laws
blocks.tag: charge at junctions, energy round loops
blocks.html:
Two laws carry every circuit that is too tangled for series and parallel alone. Both are conservation laws in disguise, and knowing WHICH one each is makes them impossible to mix up.

First, two words the laws are stated in:

  • A junction, also called a node, is a point where two or more conductors meet.
  • A loop is a closed conducting path, any route round the circuit that ends where it began.
LawStatementIt is really
Current law, at a junctionSum of currents IN equals sum of currents OUTConservation of CHARGE
Voltage law, round a loopThe sum of the voltages around any closed loop is zeroConservation of ENERGY
The hook, and it is what the exam asks for

Junctions conserve charge. Loops conserve energy.
Nothing piles up at a junction, because charge cannot be created or destroyed there.
Nothing is gained going all the way round, because you end at the same potential you started at, so the energy each coulomb gained must equal the energy it spent.

The everyday case for the current law: a river reaching a fork. Whatever flows in must flow out along the two branches. Water does not pile up at the split, and neither does charge.

The everyday case for the voltage law: a walk round a hill that returns to your front door. However much you climbed, you descended exactly the same amount, because you are back where you started.

Your turn. Three wires meet at a junction. 7 A flows in along one, 3 A flows out along another. What flows in the third, and which way?

Current law
in = out
7 = 3 + I
I = 4 A
Direction
OUT, since the ins had to balance

Nothing accumulates at the point, so the arithmetic has no choice.

blocks.label: Which resistance does the question mean?
blocks.html:
Test 1 question 12 asks for "the current that flows through R3" in a series circuit of 7, 6 and 3 ohms across 48 V.

Naming R3 invites you to compute 48/3 = 16 A. But in series the same current flows through everything, so the answer for R3 is the answer for the whole loop.

R = 7 + 6 + 3 = 16 Ω, and I = 48/16 = 3 A.

The trap works because the question sounds like it is asking about one component. It is not. In series there is only one current in the entire circuit, and naming a resistor cannot change that.

blocks.label: A mixed network, worked end to end
blocks.problem: A 12 V supply feeds a 4 Ω resistor in series with a parallel pair of 6 Ω and 12 Ω. Find the total resistance, the current from the supply, and the voltage across the parallel pair.
blocks.working:
Step 1: always collapse the PARALLEL group first

You cannot add the 4 Ω to anything until the parallel pair is a single number.

Rp = (6 x 12)/(6 + 12) = 72/18 = 4 Ω

Check: 4 is less than 6, the smaller of the pair. It passes.

Step 2: now it is a simple series circuit

Rtotal = 4 + 4 = 8 Ω

Step 3: the supply current, from Ohm's law on the whole circuit

I = V/Rtotal = 12/8 = 1.5 A

Step 4: the voltage across the parallel pair

Two routes, and they must agree.

  • Ohm's law on the group: V = I Rp = 1.5 x 4 = 6 V
  • Voltage divider: V = (Rp/Rtotal) x 12 = (4/8) x 12 = 6 V

Step 5: check with Kirchhoff's voltage law

Round the loop: 6 V across the 4 Ω resistor, plus 6 V across the pair, is 12 V, the supply. The sum round the loop is zero, as the law requires.
blocks.answer: R = 8 Ω, I = 1.5 A, and 6 V across the parallel pair
blocks.redo: Redo it asking how the 1.5 A SPLITS between the 6 Ω and the 12 Ω. Use the current divider with the OTHER resistor on top: I through the 6 Ω = (12/18) x 1.5 = 1.0 A, and I through the 12 Ω = (6/18) x 1.5 = 0.5 A. They add back to 1.5 A, as the current law demands, and the smaller resistor took the larger current.

blocks.label: Your turn
blocks.question:
(1) 10 Ω and 15 Ω in parallel. Find R, then apply the sanity check.

(2) Which Kirchhoff law is conservation of energy?

(3) In a voltage divider, which resistor goes on top?

(4) In a current divider, which resistor goes on top?
blocks.answer:
(1) R = (10 x 15)/(10 + 15) = 150/25 = 6 Ω. Less than 10, the smaller of the two, so it passes.

(2) The voltage law, round a loop. The current law at a junction is conservation of charge.

(3) The one you WANT the voltage across. Voltage goes where the resistance is.

(4) The OTHER one. Current avoids resistance, so the bigger resistor gets the smaller share, which means the other resistor sits on top.

blocks.big: Parallel is always less than the smallest
blocks.sub: Junctions conserve charge, loops conserve energy.

title: emf, Internal Resistance and Terminal Voltage
lead: One idea carries every remaining circuit question: a battery has resistance of its own, so what you measure at its terminals is always less than what it can supply.

blocks.text: The one idea behind five questions

blocks.label: Why headlights dim
blocks.html:
Start with something you have seen. Start a car at night and the headlights dip for a moment, then recover.

The battery has not gone flat. Something else happened.

  1. The starter motor suddenly drew an enormous current.
  2. A battery has resistance inside itself, called internal resistance, written as a small r.
  3. That internal resistance eats some of the battery's voltage before it ever reaches the terminals. The amount it eats is Ir.
  4. The more current you draw, the more it eats. So the lights dim.

V = ε - Ir  and  ε = I(R + r)

Key point

Whenever current flows, what you MEASURE at the terminals is always less than what the battery HAS. The gap is exactly Ir.

That measured value has a name: the terminal voltage. It is the voltage across the source while current flows, and it is always below the emf.

The one edge case worth knowing: with NO current flowing, I = 0, so Ir = 0 and the terminal voltage equals the emf exactly. That is how an emf is measured in practice, with a high-resistance voltmeter drawing almost nothing.

Your turn. A question tells you the terminal p.d. is 1 V and asks for the emf. Before any arithmetic: must your answer be bigger than 1 V, or smaller?

Answer: bigger, always.

Why
V = ε - Ir
so ε = V + Ir
and Ir is never negative
Therefore
ε is greater than V whenever current flows

That single check eliminates two of the five options on Test 2 question 4 before you calculate anything. The trap option offered is 1 V itself, the number copied straight out of the question.

Say it bluntly

What you measure is always less than what the battery has.

blocks.label: What emf actually is, and why the name is wrong
blocks.tag: a definition the exam asks for
blocks.html:
emf stands for electromotive force, and that name has misled students for a century.

Definition

emf is the energy per unit charge supplied by a source, and it is measured in VOLTS, not newtons. It is not a force at all.

Once you see that it is energy per coulomb, everything lines up:

  • A volt IS a joule per coulomb, so emf in volts is exactly energy per unit charge.
  • That is why ε and V can be subtracted from each other in V = ε - Ir. You can only subtract like from like.
  • And it is why W = ΔQ × ε from the previous lesson gives joules: charge times energy-per-charge.

The everyday picture: think of the source as a pump lifting each coulomb to a certain height. The emf is how high it lifts them. The internal resistance is a leak in the pump itself, so what actually leaves the outlet is a little lower than the lift.

blocks.label: The emf formulas
blocks.html:
QuantityFormulaNote
emf drives both resistancesε = I(R + r)The current passes through the source too
Terminal voltageV = ε - IrAlways LESS than ε
Terminal voltage, other routeV = IRIt is the voltage across the external R

What every letter means

SymbolMeaningUnit
εemf, the energy per coulomb the source can supplyvolt, V, despite the name
VTERMINAL voltage, what you would actually measure at the batteryvolt, V
ICurrent flowing round the whole circuitampere, A
RResistance of the EXTERNAL circuitohm, Ω
rINTERNAL resistance, inside the source itselfohm, Ω
Capital R and small r are the whole topic

R is outside the battery. r is inside it.
Swap them and every emf question goes wrong.
Note too that r here is a RESISTANCE, not the distance r of the electrostatics formulas. Same letter, entirely different quantity, and the only guide is which topic you are in.

blocks.label: Test 2 question 4, the two-step one
blocks.tag: hardest circuit question on the paper
blocks.problem: A cell of unknown emf ε and internal resistance 2 ohms is connected to a 5 ohm resistor. If the terminal p.d. is 1 volt, calculate ε.
blocks.working:
Given
r = 2 Ω (internal)
R = 5 Ω (external)
V = 1 V (terminal p.d.)
ε = ?

Step 1: the terminal p.d. is the voltage across the EXTERNAL resistor, so it gives you the current.
I = V/R
  = 1/5
  = 0.2 A

Step 2: the emf must push that current through BOTH resistances.
ε = I(R + r)
  = 0.2 x (5 + 2)
  = 0.2 x 7
  = 1.4 V

Check
ε = 1.4 V is greater than V = 1 V, as it must be. The difference, 0.4 V, is the internal drop Ir = 0.2 x 2. It agrees.
blocks.answer: ε = 1.4 V
blocks.redo: The offered trap is 1 V, the terminal p.d. copied straight out of the question. Whenever a question gives you a terminal p.d. and asks for emf, the answer must be BIGGER. Redo it with r = 5 ohms and confirm you get 2 V.

blocks.label: Your turn
blocks.question:
A cell has an emf of 9 V and an internal resistance of 1 ohm. The current flowing is 2 A. What is the terminal voltage?

Then, in words: what IS the terminal voltage, and what IS internal resistance?
blocks.answer:
Given
ε = 9 V
r = 1 Ω
I = 2 A

Formula
V = ε - Ir

Substitute
V = 9 - (2 x 1)
V = 9 - 2

Answer
V = 7 V

Check
7 V is LESS than the 9 V emf, as it must be.

This is the previous question run backwards: there you were given V and asked for ε, here you are given ε and asked for V. Either way the terminal voltage is the smaller of the two. An answer of 11 V would mean the internal resistance was ADDING energy, which is impossible.

In words: the terminal voltage is the voltage across a source while current flows, always less than the emf. The internal resistance is the resistance of the source itself, and it is what causes that shortfall.
